title: 东北硬菜③猪肉炖粉条：一句“馋死野狼嚎”，主角竟不是肉 | Northeast Comfort Food P3 · Pork & Glass Noodles 🍲
description:
你家的猪肉炖粉条，放酸菜还是不放？ / Your pork-and-glass-noodle stew: with pickled cabbage, or without?

第③集·猪肉炖粉条 —— 「东北硬菜」系列，每天一道东北招牌菜。
P3 · Pork & Glass Noodles — from the series Northeast Comfort Food: one Dongbei classic a day.

东北有句顺口溜：「猪肉炖粉条，馋死野狼嚎。」可这锅的主角，其实不是肉，是那把宽粉条。相传满族人为了耐寒耐饥，把土豆做成粉条，和肉一起炖——五花肉一出油，粉条最会吸，一夹起来颤巍巍地挂满汤汁，最普通的一锅，却是最下饭的一锅。讲究的人家还要加一把酸菜。它和东北「杀猪菜」同一个根：杀猪菜起于清代满族祭祀的「还愿肉」，经「还愿肉→杀年猪→杀猪菜」，慢慢变成了宴请亲友的大菜。
There's a Dongbei rhyme: “pork stewed with glass noodles makes the wolves howl.” But the real star of the pot isn't the meat — it's the wide potato-starch noodles. The story goes that the Manchus, fending off cold and hunger, turned potatoes into noodles and stewed them with pork: as the pork belly renders its fat, the noodles drink it all in, trembling and glossy when you lift them. The plainest pot, yet the one that vanishes rice fastest. The classic version adds pickled cabbage — and it shares a root with sha-zhu-cai, the northeastern “pig-slaughter feast,” which grew out of a Qing-dynasty Manchu ritual offering into a dish for entertaining guests.
